title: i've just finished my ai game demo, and here's my journey so far.
author: Candid_Discount_6834
selftext:
I just finished the demo of my 2D top-down game, and I wanted to share a little about my development experience.

I work as a forensic investigator in Brazil, and I initially came up with the idea of creating a game with Super Nintendo-style graphics to showcase at an annual geek convention held in my city.

I started brainstorming with Codex to adapt what I had in mind: an action-adventure game with a forensic investigation theme.

The engine I chose was Godot.

Sprites: This was quite difficult! I managed to create some assets with Codex, but maintaining visual consistency throughout the process is very challenging—not impossible, though. If you want to follow this approach, I suggest first creating idle sprites facing the main directions and then building the animations from there. The fewer frames an animation has, the easier it is to generate. Generate the images until they are as close as possible to what you want; you will need to adjust the details in an editor afterward. I used LibreSprite for that.

I created the first demo using this workflow, but for the current version I used pixellab to make the artwork more consistent overall.

Maps and assets: In the first demo, I generated a flat PNG and used it as the map. However, the player’s interaction with objects was limited because everything was on a single object layer. As a result, walking in front of or behind objects did not look very good, and shader-based animations did not work as well either.

The solution was to create the entire map with all the assets, then use the SAM2 masking tool to separate the objects and place them on top of the map as individual layers. This made the map much easier to animate and edit.

Music: This part was quite simple. I used Gemini’s music generation tool to create something that suited my taste.

Code: All the code was generated by Codex using the GODOT AI plugin, which made the changes directly inside the program. It is important to use a tool like this because it creates the scenes inside the project as if a user were operating the program. If you use Codex or Claude Code to make these changes, they will modify the project directly through code, which makes it harder to visualize and edit things within the project manually.

That’s it for my journey. I hope you can get something useful from my experience.

My game, Operation Evidence, is available for download for free on itch.io (https://opevidence.itch.io/operation-evidence). Anyone who wants to try it out and share feedback is very welcome.

Thank you, everyone.
